Thanks, Evelyn — attaching a short sample export (hyperion_traffic_sample.csv). High-level answers inline below and in the CSV:

- Steady-state: 120 requests/sec (business hours)
- Peak: 480 requests/sec for roughly 2-3 hours during batch clinical analysis windows (happens ~2x/week)
- Average tokens per request: 280 tokens (input+output). p95 ~ 560 tokens.
- Streaming: ~50% of requests use streaming (progressive results), average streamed output ~512 tokens per streamed call
- SLO: p95 latency target <= 300 ms for non-streaming requests; streaming can tolerate slightly higher per-chunk latency but overall responsiveness should feel <500ms for first token
- Compliance: US-only data residency required; we plan to buy Dedicated with a VPC (no on-prem initially)
- Commitment: looking at a 12-month reserved purchase if sizing and pricing fit

Question: can you provide two options — one optimized for latency (lower model size / quantization) and one for quality (70B family) — with estimated GPUs, headroom, and expected p95 latency? Also please flag any caching or prefix reuse strategies that will materially reduce capacity needs.

Thanks,

From: Evelyn Hart <evelyn.hart@redwood.ai>
To: Marcus Lin <marcus.lin@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 10 Sep 2026 14:02:05 -0700
Subject: Fwd: Hyperion - dedicated capacity sizing follow-up

Marcus / Karthik — forwarding Hyperion's traffic sample and the asks. Quick top-line from my read: steady tokens/sec = 120 * 280 = 33,600 t/s; peak tokens/sec = 480 * 280 = 134,400 t/s (p95 token size pushes that higher briefly). They want two options: latency-optimized (likely 13B quantized) and quality-focused (70B family). They also asked about caching/prefix reuse.

Could you run a rough sized recommendation using Redwood runtime assumptions and the hardware we offer in Dedicated (H100-80GB pool). For the note below, assume:
- 13B (8-bit quant) on H100: ~5,500 tokens/sec/GPU (sustained on Redwood runtime, optimized kernels)
- 70B (int8) on H100: ~1,400 tokens/sec/GPU
- Cache/prefix reuse reductions: realistic 15-25% token reduction depending on prompt overlap; use 20% as baseline
- Target headroom: 1.5x for burst tolerance and maintenance windows

Rough math I started: 
- Steady tokens/sec: 33,600 t/s -> with 20% caching -> effective 26,880 t/s
- Peak tokens/sec: 134,400 t/s -> with 20% caching -> effective 107,520 t/s

GPUs required (before rounding):
- 13B: peak 107,520 / 5,500 ≈ 19.6 -> with 1.5x headroom ≈ 29.4 => recommend 30 GPUs (H100)
- 70B: peak 107,520 / 1,400 ≈ 76.8 -> with 1.5x headroom ≈ 115.2 => recommend 116 GPUs (H100)

Latency estimate (p95 non-streaming):
- 13B @ 30 GPUs: expected p95 ≈ 160-220 ms (network + runtime + kernel), fits their 300 ms SLO comfortably
- 70B @ 116 GPUs: expected p95 ≈ 220-320 ms (depends on tail; may slightly exceed 300 ms at very high concurrency)

Operational recommendations:
- Recommend baseline reserved pool = 30x H100 (13B ops) if Hyperion prioritizes latency and cost predictability.
- Offer an upsell path: 116x H100 pool for 70B quality; this is large and drives high commit pricing — present as optional phase 2.
- Autoscale/burst plan: enable autoscale to add +30% burst capacity from a shared burst pool or use on-demand fallback to hosted instances for short peaks (2-3 hours).
- Caching: implement prefix caching and KV reuse for common prompts — we estimate ~20% effective token reduction and fewer GPUs required.
- Canary: start with a 7-day canary at 30 GPUs in a dedicated tenant, measure real p95 and effective caching factor, then expand.

Can you validate the per-GPU throughput assumptions and adjust if you think they’re off? Also adding the Hyperion CSV and a quick sizing calc would be helpful to include in the quote.

Thanks — I’ll respond to Sara once we have engineering numbers to attach to the commercial proposal.

–Evelyn
From: Marcus Lin <marcus.lin@redwood.ai>
To: Evelyn Hart <evelyn.hart@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 11 Sep 2026 14:22:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Fwd: Hyperion - dedicated capacity sizing follow-up

Evelyn / Karthik — quick sanity-check and a slightly adjusted recommendation attached (Hyperion_GPU_sizing_calc.xlsx). Notes below: 

1) Throughput adjustments:
- Measured throughput numbers used in prior runs (Redwood internal perf bench): 13B int8 @ ~5,200 t/s on H100 (sustained); 70B int8 @ ~1,300 t/s. I trimmed the 13B number by ~6% to be conservative.

2) Effective caching: agree 20% baseline, but call out a range (15%-30%). If Hyperion confirms >25% prompt reuse we should reduce reserved pool accordingly.

3) Revised GPU counts (rounded up to whole machines + maintenance spare):
- 13B path: peak_eff 107,520 t/s / 5,200 ≈ 20.7 GPUs -> +50% headroom = 31.0 -> recommend 32 GPUs (include 2 spare nodes for upgrades/rolling restarts).
- 70B path: peak_eff 107,520 / 1,300 ≈ 82.7 -> +50% headroom = 124.0 -> recommend 128 GPUs (allocate in # of machines to match rack configs).

4) Latency expectations:
- 13B @ 32 GPUs: p95 non-streaming ≈ 140-200 ms. Streaming first-token latency ≈ 120-180 ms. Good margin vs 300 ms SLO.
- 70B @ 128 GPUs: p95 non-streaming ≈ 200-320 ms (tight at peak). If Hyperion needs firm 300 ms p95 at all times, we should either increase the 70B pool or use model sharding/hybrid routing (route latency-critical calls to 13B).

5) Cost/ops notes:
- 13B reserve (32x H100) is the pragmatic recommendation for guaranteed SLO + 12-month commit. This keeps price/throughput favorable and reduces committed spend vs the 70B option.
- 70B reserve only if Hyperion values LLM output quality substantially more and is comfortable with higher commit. Consider offering a hybrid: reserve 32x H100 + an on-demand 70B fleet for quality-only scoring or offline batch runs.

6) Deliverables for the quote: 
- Formal sizing table (attached)
- Canary run plan & success criteria (p95 <= 300ms, effective caching >= 15%)
- Fallback policy (route to hosted fallback if >95th percentile burst beyond reserved)

I'll attach the sizing workbook and a short Jupyter with the simulation (SLA_Simulation.ipynb) for their review. If you want, I can also produce a simple visual showing token/sec over a sample week and the capacity envelope.

Marcus Lin
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
